scenes.title: The Bloop
scenes.text: In 1997, something in the Pacific Ocean made a sound so loud, it was picked up by sensors more than five thousand kilometres apart.

scenes.title: Listening for submarines
scenes.text: The underwater microphones were built to listen for submarines. They had never heard anything like this.

scenes.title: The real recording
scenes.text: It rose fast and was far too powerful for any known animal. Listen.

scenes.title: A sea monster?
scenes.text: Many people believed it came from a giant, unknown creature in the deep.

scenes.title: NOAA's answer
scenes.text: Years later, scientists gave their answer: an icequake. A huge iceberg cracking and breaking away from Antarctica.

scenes.title: Would you go down there?
scenes.text: But for years, nobody knew what made it. Would you go down and look?

scenes.title: The Taos Hum
scenes.text: In Taos, a small desert town in New Mexico, some people hear a sound that others cannot hear.

scenes.title: A distant engine
scenes.text: A low, steady rumble, like a diesel engine idling far away. Day and night.

scenes.title: Who hears it?
scenes.text: In a survey in the 1990s, about two percent of the people living there said they could hear it.

scenes.title: Scientists came
scenes.text: Scientists came with sensitive microphones and instruments. They could not find where it comes from.

scenes.title: Can you hear it?
scenes.text: The ground, power lines, or something inside the ears of the people who hear it? Nobody knows. Would you want to hear it?

scenes.title: The Wow! Signal
scenes.text: On August fifteenth, 1977, a radio telescope in Ohio caught a signal from deep space.

scenes.title: The hydrogen line
scenes.text: It was strong and narrow, right next to the radio frequency of hydrogen, where scientists thought an alien message might be sent.

scenes.title: "Wow!"
scenes.text: Astronomer Jerry Ehman circled it on the printout and wrote one word: Wow!

scenes.title: 72 seconds
scenes.text: It lasted seventy two seconds, and came from the direction of the constellation Sagittarius.

scenes.title: It never came back
scenes.text: Astronomers have searched that spot for decades. It has never come back. Was it a message?

scenes.title: The Voynich Manuscript
scenes.text: This book is about six hundred years old, and nobody on Earth can read it.

scenes.title: Early 1400s
scenes.text: Carbon dating puts its pages in the early fourteen hundreds.

scenes.title: An unknown alphabet
scenes.text: It is written in an alphabet that appears nowhere else in the world.

scenes.title: Plants that don't exist
scenes.text: Its pages are full of plants nobody can identify, star charts, and strange drawings of bathing women.

scenes.title: Still unbroken
scenes.text: Codebreakers, linguists and even computers have tried. No one has cracked it.

scenes.title: Could you read it?
scenes.text: Today it is kept at Yale University. Do you think anyone will ever read it?
